item.title: ELI STEELE: France's schools are burning. White guilt is helping fan the flames
item.description: A burning school in Nantes and Palestinian flags in the streets reveal how White guilt fuels France's student protests, author and filmmaker Eli Steele argues
item.content:encoded:
Editor's note: This op-ed is part of a series by Eli Steele exploring White guilt in America and the West. Steele is the director of the newly released documentary essay, "White Guilt." See the film at WhiteGuiltFilm.com.

One of the most striking images of the riots that I saw sweeping France in recent days was that of a burning school in Nantes. The student movement in the streets around the school called itself a demand for education.

I was scrolling through my X feed when I saw the image of a burning trash can outside Lycée Nelson Mandela. The flames spread to the walls of the building and into the glass entrance hall. There were still students in their classrooms and, thankfully, every one of them got out.

When this school opened 12 years ago, its construction cost approximately €64 million, and it was touted as a beacon of hope and possibility for young people. Now the school has been shuttered for repairs, and its 1,700 students must learn from home for the time being.

TRUMP, WALTZ LINK FRANCE RIOTS TO MASS IMMIGRATION AS THOUSANDS ARE ARRESTED

And that is just one school. According to the education minister, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since late September, and about 30,000 students won't see the inside of their classrooms for weeks. More than 6,500 people have been arrested, most of them minors. At least 215 students have been hurt, along with 85 teachers and staff. A 16-year-old lost the use of an eye. In La Ciotat, a physics teacher was sprayed in the face with gasoline and struck by a student from his own lycée while trying to put out a fire.

Many media figures and nonprofit organizations like Amnesty International emphasized the students’ demands for better educational conditions and criticized the police response, while also acknowledging violence by some demonstrators. The demands were for more teachers, smaller classes, and decent buildings.

FRENCH PM REJECTS POLICE BRUTALITY CLAIMS AFTER TEENS SEVERELY INJURED IN PROTESTS: 'ACCIDENTS HAPPEN'

In the more shocking videos that flowed from the streets of France out into the world, there were teachers who made a point of standing with the students in the streets. In some cases, parents and union members joined in. The mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, stood with students who were blockading their own school and argued that violence can sometimes be legitimate, although he also said he opposed violence and called for de-escalation.

As one watches the footage of students swarming the streets, seemingly with impunity, one has to wonder how the civilization that gave the world Voltaire, Rousseau, Camus and the free public school arrived at a place where schools can burn amid a movement demanding better schools.

FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT

In more ways than one, this is just an old story. A post-1960s story. What is happening in the streets of France is the latest iteration of the White guilt formula that has its roots in America.

My father, Shelby Steele, has written about White guilt since the 1980s. For him, White guilt is not personal. It is not the guilt a person feels for something he did. Almost no Whites alive today owned slaves or ran colonies. How can one feel guilt for sins one did not commit?

ELI STEELE: THE TERROR OF BEING CALLED RACIST IS CRUSHING FREE SPEECH IN AMERICA

White guilt is collective guilt. The left has condemned all Whites for the sins of the West, from slavery and segregation to colonialism. It has made whiteness a symbol of historical evil that must be torn down. In doing so, it has created the terror of being called a racist or a colonialist and stripped of moral authority. To escape that terror, many Whites try to buy their way out. But only the "oppressed" can grant innocence, and so a bargain is struck. The "oppressed" sell victimhood for power. The "oppressor" buys innocence with deference, programs, and lower expectations, and when the pressure is high enough, silence in the face of the match. Both sides get what they want, except the children, who are mere pawns.

There is a difference between then and now. In the 1960s, people were oppressed. Today they are taught oppression. Most of these students never lived under colonialism. They have been taught that they still do. So, we should not be surprised, and yet it is still startling, that one of the main features of these protests has often been the Palestinian flag. A flag about Gaza has nothing to do with class sizes in Nantes, and yet it says everything about this movement.

ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'

It does two things at once. First, it is an accusation. The students have been taught that Israel is the genocidal oppressor and the Palestinians their innocent victims. When they raise that flag, they are accusing France of being like Israel. Second, it is the claim that the students are the Palestinians in this situation and therefore they are the inheritors of the victimhood that the flag symbolizes. They have granted themselves innocence and moral legitimacy through victimhood.

When the Saint-Denis mayor claims that violence can be legitimate, he is merely following the script of the Black Lives Matter activists who called the 2020 looting across America reparations. If he stood against the students and demanded the Western values of responsibility and accountability, he would be branded a traitor to the cause. After all, the victims must remain victims.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The blockades have spread from the suburbs into Paris, all the way to the most elite lycées in France, and even private schools. These private school students come from comparatively privileged backgrounds and, judging from the photos of the barricades, many are White. White guilt rewards even the White students if they do one key thing: dissociate from the evil West. Their reward for allying with the oppressed is innocence.

No matter what France does, it loses. Every attempt by the "oppressor system" to restore law and order becomes a new grievance for the oppressed. When one insists that a newish €64 million school is not a symbol of neglect, one is cast out with contempt as a racist. When a care worker at a Marseille bus stop told students not to smash the shelter and to go protest instead, a 15-year-old fired a flaming spray into her face. Afterward, she still called their cause "noble, legitimate."

The "oppressed" will never give up the grievance, because under White guilt it is their only power. The White guilt elites only care about the innocence they gain from escaping the oppressor box via allyship. After all, they see their own nation as the oppressor. So the decline continues.

What burned in Nantes was not just the school. It was the idea that a nation can defend itself, its laws and principles without first confessing to its past sins. White guilt makes that defense difficult, if not impossible. And that is what gives White guilt its power as the most destructive force in America and the West. It turns the people who built the school into the people who watch it burn and call it social justice.

item.title: MLB proposes reverting schedule back to its old ways, but not without a wild postseason twist
item.description: Major League Baseball's proposal includes a 154-game season with weekly off-days and a best-of-seven Division Series starting as early as 2029.
item.content:encoded:
With a second lockout this decade pending, Major League Baseball owners are coming up with creative ways to get on the baseball field as planned in 2027.

The league announced the proposal of a 154-game season, which would knock out eight games of the 162-game slate that was implemented in 1961.

Owners also proposed the Division Series, which has been a best-of-five since its introduction in 1995, to be a best-of-seven, but with a wild twist.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The highest seed in both the Wild Card and Division Series, owners proposed, would be given the ability to choose their opponents.

"Returning to a 154-game schedule would allow us to introduce a weekly off-day, which is good for player health, while also creating a new national broadcast window to showcase our most exciting teams and players," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said. "A shorter regular season unlocks making October even better for our fans -- with fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series and more opportunities to see the game’s best pitchers on the biggest stage. And allowing the top seeds to select their opponents in the first two rounds would create compelling storylines, intensify existing rivalries and create new ones."

The opponent-choosing could perhaps be a reaction to this year's postseason format, in which the American League teams with the second- and third-best records, the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox, will not see the Championship Series.

YANKEES LEGENDS DEREK JETER, ALEX RODRIGUEZ DELIVER BLUNT POST-MORTEM ON TEAM: 'SOMETHING HAS TO CHANGE'

Under the current format, rather than reseeding , the top seed in each league is automatically slated to face the winner of the 4-5 seed matchup, and the No. 2 seed goes against the 3-6 seed winner. The top three seeds are given to the three division winners (with the top two getting a bye), in record order, while the 4-6 seeds are given to the best non-division winners, also in record order. Thus, despite the second-best record in the AL, the Yankees were the fourth seed.

With the 154-game schedule, which wouldn't be implemented until 2029, all teams would be off on Mondays , except for a rare nationally televised game or a holiday, in which case they would then be off that Thursday. Minor League Baseball is off every Monday, which has apparently been well received , as it's normally paired with a Sunday day game.

Each team would also have a scheduled split doubleheader against each of its division rivals during the season.

MLB teams originally played 154 games until the 1960s.

The proposal from the owners still includes a salary cap, which players have adamantly opposed and said is non-negotiable. The owners are expected to lock out the players on Dec. 1, when the current collective bargaining agreement expires.

item.title: Lindsey Vonn works up a sweat for her birthday, Dodgers slammed for celebration & Romo's bad stretch continues
item.description: Lindsey Vonn gears up for her 42nd birthday with a flurry of summer content as Jazz Chisholm struggles to explain why Yankees fans booed him.
item.content:encoded:
Over the hump and safely on the other side! We've got football tonight. We've got more playoff baseball. We've got a Yankees-less October to look forward to now!

What a time to be alive. If we could only get the Dodgers outta here, it would be perfect.

Give me White Sox-Brewers for all the marbles, just like God intended!

On that note, welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Lindsey Vonn works up a sweat as she gears up for a big birthday bash.

LINDSEY VONN TURNS HEADS BY HER POOL, GISELE SNUBS TOM BRADY & THE RIDICULOUS FAKE OUTRAGE OVER US OPEN FANS

Happy early 42nd birthday, Lindsey!

What else? I've got Jazz Chisholm confused as to why he was booed last night, Ronald Acuna NOT confused as to why he was booed, and Tony Romo's baaaaaaaaaaaaaaad stretch continued last weekend at a Korn Ferry qualifier.

TONY ROMO HIT WITH SEVERAL NEW CITATIONS AFTER OWI ARREST, FURTHER JEOPARDIZING RETURN TO NFL BROADCASTS

Poor Tony got the two most feared letters in the alphabet scribbled on his scorecard after the final round. You'll see.

OK, grab you a big 'ol drink, pour it out for the Yankees, and then settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

Let's go ahead and get on with the big story of the day on this second Thursday of October ...

Was that Anthony Volpe home run ... a home run?

I say no, it was not. The first replay is deceiving, but the second one from the side makes it pretty clear. I think the umps got it 100% right.

"But statcast said it would've been a home run, Zach!"

Yeah, well my eyes said it wouldn't have been a home run, and I'm still taking actual humans over the robots in 2026. Maybe not in 2027, but certainly in 2026.

And by the way, for those too young to remember ... last night was a makeup call from the Baseball Gods 30 years (!!!) in the making:

Yeah, I don't want to hear it, Yankees fans. You were always living on borrowed time after that.

Now that we've got that outta the way, let's go ahead and get this class started with Lindsey Vonn gearing up for her 42nd birthday:

"I guess this means summer is over….but it also means my birthday is coming up soon," Vonn wrote before dumping out a flurry of Instagram content from this past summer.

Amen, Lindsey! What a year for OutKick's favorite Olympian. Scrambled her leg back in February, had everything patched up, and now she's on the comeback tour as we close in on Halloween.

I would expect nothing less. She's a champion. If I'm buying stock in 2027, it's gonna be in Lindsey Vonn. I think she's got more in the tank.

I can't wait to find out.

Moving on ...

Let's head BACK to Yankee Stadium and check in with Jazz Chisholm after last night's dud in New York.

Jazz, for those who missed it, was confused as to why Yankees fans booed the hell out of him after grounding out in the bottom of the ninth.

Seems like a real head-scratcher to me!

"It doesn't hurt. It's just confusing because it's the playoffs and we're trying to win games. So you're booing a guy that's playing trying to help the team win."

Hey, Jazz — if you don't wanna be booed, maybe head back down to Miami! I despise the Yankees, but I can absolutely understand why the fans booed you for swinging at a 1-0 pitch, after five straight balls, with the tying run on first in the final inning.

You can't figure out why they booed you for that? Really? Come on.

Now, I'm not the biggest Ronald Acuna fan after these playoffs, either, but goodness, just look at how HE responded to being booed last night:

I thought Acuna looked checked out the entire postseason. Believe me, I've watched every Braves game because the First Lady is a Braves fan. He looked disinterested from the jump.

But at least he owned it after another horrible game last night. Take notes, Jazz!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big Thursday night. First up? Might as well stay on the diamond and check in with the NLDS champion Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers!

I've noticed this a bunch in sports over the past few years ... the celebrations seem far more toned down than I can ever remember.

Fair or foul?

Obviously, everyone is gonna pick on the Dodgers here because they're low-hanging fruit, but the Brewers were just as guilty last night. Perhaps it's the whole, "Act like you've been there before" mindset, which certainly applies to LA. They are quite literally there every year.

I was a little surprised at the Brewers, though. That was an intense series, and a hostile environment. I thought I'd see a little more out of them.

Oh well. Brew Crew in six!

Finally, on the way out, let's check in with Tony Romo fresh off his ... amicable departure ... from CBS:

Hilarious story from a Korn Ferry pre-qualifier in Oklahoma.

Apparently, Tony Romo shaved two strokes off his final round scorecard. Inadvertently, of course.

He put himself down for pars on the 16th and 17th hole on his final back-nine, when his playing partner — a pro from Louisiana named Brandon Rice — had him at bogeys for both holes.

Rice told Monday Q Info earlier this week that he thought Romo made a 5 on his 16th hole, but Romo told him in scoring it actually was a 4, and that’s the score Romo signed for.

Romo's group was also being monitored by a South Central PGA pro because it was "limping" to the finish, according to the unnamed pro. The same pro told GOLF.com that Romo had a three-putt bogey 5 on 16 and a three-putt bogey 5 on 17.

Not good!

Keller, a former All-American college golfer and a widely respected rules official, described a rushed scoring process and Romo signing Rice’s proffered card without carefully checking it," GOLF.com wrote. "He suggested that Romo, between the slow-play warning hanging over the group, his inability to mount any sort of birdie run 'and all that was going on with him' was frustrated with how the day went.

"Keller said Romo took responsibility for the wrong card and was 'very complimentary' about the event and how it was run. Keller noted that Romo was not going to advance either way."

Just an awful run of luck for Tony Romo right now. He gets dinged for a pesky OWI, loses his job at CBS, and then gets outed by some nark in Oklahoma.

Oh well. They say bad things come in threes, which means Tony is about to turn this thing around at the buzzer.

Stay tuned!

OK, that's it for today. Good class. Long class. Let's go have a big Thursday night of football, and get ready for a monster weekend.

Let's end the day with MORE golf, this time in the form of Paige Spiranac and bunch of other influencers I don't know and hope to never know.

See you Friday.

item.description: An MV-22B Osprey burst into flames after a hard landing near Bladen Lakes State Forest, with at least one person aboard reportedly suffering burns.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S. Marine Corps aircraft carrying four service members burst into flames Thursday following a hard landing during a training mission in North Carolina.

The MV-22B Osprey out of Marine Corps Air Station New River went down near the Bladen Lakes State Forest.

BLOODIED, EJECTED MARINE CORPS PILOT SEEN CALM AND COLLECTED AFTER WASHINGTON CRASH DESTROYS AIRCRAFT

All four personnel aboard were taken for medical evaluation, according to a Marine Corps statement provided to Fox News. White Lake Fire Chief Dale Brennan told WECT that at least one Marine suffered burns and was rushed to a nearby clinic.

Both civilian and military emergency crews responded to the site.

item.title: Nebraska Christian therapists sue city over ban on helping minors accept their biological sex
item.description: The Thomas More Society claims Lincoln, Nebraska's, ordinance threatens therapists with jail and fines for helping minors address unwanted same-sex attraction.
item.content:encoded:
Christian counselors are suing Lincoln, Nebraska, over an ordinance they say threatens therapists with jail, fines and professional consequences for helping minors who want to become comfortable with their biological sex or address unwanted same-sex attraction, even after the Supreme Court struck down a similar Colorado restriction earlier this year.

Thomas More Society Senior Counsel Matt Heffron told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that Lincoln's ordinance amounts to government "viewpoint discrimination," arguing counselors are permitted to help minors move toward gender transition but are barred from counseling them toward accepting their biological sex when that is the client's stated goal.

"The government allows certain type of speech in therapy sessions, and it disallows other sorts of speech or viewpoints," Heffron said. "It's just a confirmation of government viewpoint, government-favored speech over disfavored speech."

FIRED SCHOOL COUNSELOR LOSES AGAIN AFTER FREE SPEECH FIGHT OVER GENDER-THEMED BOOKS IN HIS OFFICE

Heffron said Lincoln's ordinance prevents counselors from helping minors who want to become comfortable with their biological sex or address unwanted same-sex attraction.

He argued that a nearly identical Colorado restriction was found unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Chiles v. Salazar as viewpoint discrimination and that the 8th Circuit subsequently reached a similar conclusion in a case involving Kansas City.

EXCLUSIVE: INDIANA SCHOOL COUNSELOR FIRED FOR SPEAKING OUT ON GENDER IDENTITY POLICY SETTLES LAWSUIT FOR $200K

Heffron said a counselor accused of having those conversations could face an investigation and potentially a misdemeanor charge, a $500 fine, a $100 civil penalty and the loss of professional licenses or credentials.

Heffron said the Thomas More Society repeatedly asked Lincoln to repeal the ordinance or agree not to enforce it. So, after the city declined to do so and stopped responding, the group filed suit.

DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS

"The stakes of this case, as far as minors are concerned, is that there are minors out there, and a fair number of them is what I hear, who are, perhaps faith-based or for other reasons, they are unhappy with same-sex attraction that they may be experiencing, or they're unhappy with what used to be called gender dysphoria," Heffron said.

"And these minors go to a therapist, particularly a Catholic one like the one in this case, and they ask to be helped. It's awful. It's cruel to tell those children they can't be helped. 

"In fact, the only thing that the statute or that ordinance allows is it will allow that therapist to help guide them into gender transition with all of the evils that include surgeries and hormones and that sort of thing. They can guide them into that. And they can make them comfortable with their same-sex attraction."

CATHOLIC NUNS CARING FOR DYING PATIENTS FIGHT NEW YORK TRANS RULE, FACE JAIL TIME

In this instance, Heffron said the government is policing speech.

"When an ordinance tries to say what sort of view is allowed, what sort of speech is allowed, that's viewpoint discrimination," Heffron said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Jamie Reyes, director of the Lincoln Commission on Human Rights in Lincoln, Nebraska, for comment. The city said that it does not comment on pending litigation.

item.title: Former US Open golf champion Corey Pavin announces wife's cancer 'never went away completely'
item.description: Corey Pavin revealed his wife Lisa's cancer never fully went away and she is now undergoing CAR-T therapy at the Mayo Clinic after chemotherapy.
item.content:encoded:
Professional golfer Corey Pavin announced that his wife Lisa has to return to the hospital for cancer treatments after her original cancer "never went away completely."

The 1995 US Open champion revealed back in February that Lisa, 52, completed her final round of chemotherapy treatments, however, on Tuesday, Pavin posted on social media that she was set to undergo more cell-based gene therapy treatment.

Neither Pavin nor his wife have revealed the exact type of cancer she is currently battling.

"Seven plus months ago, I posted that (Lisa) had her last chemotherapy," Pavin wrote in a post on Instagram. "We found out a couple months ago that her cancer never went away completely."

Despite the gut punch diagnosis, Pavin appears to be optimistic about the outlook based on his words online.

CANCER VACCINE PREVENTS DEADLY MELANOMA FROM RETURNING OR SPREADING IN LANDMARK TRIAL

"Over the last two months and after multiple visits to The Mayo Clinic, Lisa is getting her CAR-T infusion today. We are hoping and praying that this will kick her cancer’s a–!"

Pavin writes that the emotional and physical toll of fighting the disease has been taxing while praising Lisa for her "courage" and showing plenty of gratitude towards the doctors as well as the family's support group.

REITAN WINS AFTER NEARLY QUITTING FOR YOUTUBE, SNEDEKER'S WELL-EARNED CRY, AND EARLY PGA CHAMPIONSHIP HYPE

"To the doctors, nurses and everyone at The Mayo Clinic, a heartfelt thank you for your care and empathy," he writes.

"And much gratitude to all of Lisa’s friends who have reached out to her for your prayers and support which has helped more than you will ever know!"

The comments are all universally positive and supportive, with followers offering prayers and words of encouragement , including former athletes such as Troy Aikman, Kenny Lofton and Teemu Selane.

Even during his wife's battle, Pavin has found time to play the game he loves.

The former US Open champion took part in the Sanford International at Minnehaha Country Club in Sioux Falls, South Dakota last month, finishing 21 strokes behind eventual winner Zach Johnson.

item.title: Jon Stewart tells Democrats to 'govern' and skip 'performative' Trump impeachment if they win
item.description: Jon Stewart warned Democrats against the "performative play" of impeaching President Donald Trump, urging the party to govern and fix the issues killing people now.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Jon Stewart urged Democrats not to pursue impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump if they regain control of the House and Senate, arguing on his podcast that he doesn't want to see "performative" hearings.

During a question-and-answer segment at the end of Stewart's "The Weekly Show" podcast, he was asked whether Democrats should seek to impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress in the midterm elections.

He said he wanted to see Democrats make a full-scale effort to rebalance the economy, and said he didn't want to see performative hearings.

"I don't want to see a f---ing five-act performative play of House hearings," Stewart said. "I just don't want to see it. I don't want to see everybody having the opportunity to pantomime accountability because you know they're actually not going to bring it."

STEWART EXPECTS SCHUMER, JEFFRIES TO DISAPPOINT IF THE DEMS WIN BACK THE HOUSE AND SENATE

"You want to do some investigations of some s---, that's great," he continued. "But on the triage list of what's wrong in this country, it is, 'I'm sorry, sir, you're going to have to stay in the waiting room because this guy just got shot, and it sounds to me like you just have a sore throat.' Like do the s--- that actually is killing people right now."

Stewart added that he wanted Democrats to "govern."

"You want to do some things that are ancillary, a little side project, you want to do the investigations as a hobby, knock yourself out. Fix s---," he said.

"Jon Stewart is tapping into a real tension within the Democratic electorate," Lauryn Killian, CEO of Killian Campaigns, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "There will certainly be Democrats who want impeachment, particularly those who believe the Trump administration warrants aggressive congressional scrutiny."

"But there is a meaningful difference between legitimate accountability and turning impeachment into another chapter of the anti-Trump resistance movement," she continued. "If Democrats take back Congress, voters will expect them to actually govern, not spend two years trying to undo the last election." 

HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY

Killian said the smarter political strategy would be to look into "wrongdoing and pursue accountability where the facts warrant it, while focusing congressional energy on issues that actually affect Americans' lives: the economy, affordability, public safety and government competence."

"Winning Congress would give Democrats an opportunity to demonstrate they can govern beyond simply being the opposition," she added. "If they turn that opportunity into another impeachment crusade, Republicans will have a very clear argument to make to voters: Democrats were given power to govern, and chose instead to keep fighting the last election." 

"Jon Stewart is saying what Democrats don't want to hear: voters want results, not revenge," Y. David Scharf, chair of government strategies and controversies at Morrison Cohen, told Fox News Digital. "If Democrats win Congress and spend the next two years trying to impeach Trump instead of lowering costs and fixing the economy, they'll be writing the Republican playbook for 2028."

He described impeachment as "political theater."

Democratic strategist James Carville and his podcast co-host Al Hunt also warned against impeachment on Tuesday. Carville and Hunt argued that impeachment would be a waste of time and Democrats should devote their energy to investigating the president instead.

CARVILLE SAYS THE GOP IS BETTER THAN DEMOCRATS AT ONE KEY SKILL THE 2028 DEM NOMINEE WILL NEED

"I’ll tell you one thing that I think Democrats should steer clear of, and that’s impeachment," Hunt said. "It’s not that Trump has not committed impeachable offenses, far worse than what he was accused of back in 2019 with Ukraine. I mean, he has. I mean, you could come up with a bill of particulars of, you know, a dozen at least. But you know something, James? It’s not going to happen, and it is a distraction."

"It is a waste of energy," Hunt added. "Investigate, investigate, investigate. Don’t go on a mission that isn’t going to succeed."

Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who also served as White House chief of staff, urged fellow Democrats not to pursue impeachment during an interview on Sunday.

"You’re never going to get an impeachment," he said. "Then, if you do that, you just basically prove all [of] Washington is what the American people think. It’s Disneyland on the Potomac. Deliver the change. Deliver a comprehensive ethics package that uses the investigations to then deliver change."

The warnings came as Democrats held a polling advantage over Republicans heading into the final weeks before the midterm elections.

FORMER CHICAGO MAYOR RAHM EMANUEL DECLARES AMERICA IS READY FOR A JEWISH PRESIDENT

House race projections show Democrats winning 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning Democrats would need to win at least three of the 19 remaining toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has declined to say whether he would support impeachment proceedings against Trump, though he appeared to suggest over the summer that impeachment would not be a top priority.

Fox News' Anders Hagstrom and Alexander Hall contributed to this report.

item.title: Schumer, Jeffries dodge Mamdani controversy as fellow New York Dem unloads
item.description: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's Oct. 7 anniversary statement drew sharp criticism, but Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have stayed notably silent.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has come under fire for his comments on the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, but two leading voices in New York politics have so far remained quiet.

Mamdani’s post on Wednesday briefly acknowledged Hamas’ blitz on Israel that left more than 1,100 Israelis dead and more than 250 others captured and held hostage by the terrorist organization. But the bulk of his statement spent time on criticizing Israel for its actions in Gaza in the three years since.

"The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children," Mamdani said on X. "Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed."

MAMDANI DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-ISRAEL OCT 7 STATEMENT AFTER BACKLASH

"That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing," he continued. "Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes."

Mamdani notably did not mention the Jewish community in New York City, which is home to nearly 1 million Jews, according to a 2023 study from the UJA-Federation of New York.

And while at least one New York Democrat, Rep. Dan Goldman, laid into Mamdani for his comments, neither Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer nor House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the two most powerful Democrats in Congress, has reacted.

MAMDANI’S $30M PLAN TO FIGHT ANTISEMITISM INCLUDES INCREASED FUNDING FOR ANTI-ISRAEL GROUP

"This is a reprehensible statement on the anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack by a Palestinian terrorist organization against innocent Israelis," Goldman said on X. "In the guise of ‘grieving’ with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with."

Neither Schumer nor Jeffries responded to requests for comment on Mamdani's remarks. They put out their own statements on the Oct. 7 attack on Wednesday.

Schumer, who is Jewish, noted that the attack was the "single deadliest day in Jewish history since the Holocaust." His support of Israel has become a wedge issue for some Senate Democrats, who have slowly pushed back against funding arms for Israel following three years of conflict in Gaza.

DEM SENATOR WHO DEMANDED SAUDI ACCOUNTABILITY OVER KHASHOGGI MEETS WITH CROWN PRINCE, PUSHES PALESTINIAN STATE

"Today, we reaffirm our commitment to the security of the Israeli people, to the aid and wellbeing of the Palestinian people and the recovery of the devastation in Gaza that the ensuing conflict brought, and to doubling down on efforts for a lasting peace resulting in two states where Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in equal measures of peace, security, dignity, and mutual recognition," Schumer said.

Jeffries was more aligned with Schumer’s left flank in his statement, while recognizing that "we are reminded of the painful reality that the Jewish people are in a constant struggle for survival, as has been the case for thousands of years."

"Throughout the past three years, considerable suffering has plagued the Middle East. The horrific death of Palestinian civilians, destruction of civil society and devastation in Gaza is reprehensible and can never be allowed to happen again," Jeffries said.

"In order to end the vicious cycle of bloodshed, for the good of the Israeli and Palestinian people, American policy in the region must change dramatically," he continued. "We must commit to the creation of an independent Palestinian state to provide dignity, respect and self-determination for the Palestinian people."

item.title: Israeli actress calls out Hollywood stars 'silencing artists' who support Jewish state
item.description: Noa Cohen pushed back against Hollywood celebrities calling for boycotts of Israeli film institutions, saying "silencing artists" closes conversation.
item.content:encoded:
Israeli actress Noa Cohen pushed back against celebrities "silencing artists" supporting the Jewish state, according to comments reported by The Hollywood Reporter Wednesday.

Cohen spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about her latest film, "Our Loves," a drama set during the deadly Oct. 7 terror attacks in 2023. 

The film, one of the first to dramatize the events, drew criticism for being told largely through Israeli citizens' perspectives as Hollywood stars continue to speak out against Israel.

The 24-year-old actress, who knew many victims of the Hamas attacks, expressed dismay at celebrities' actions, particularly their calls to boycott Israeli film institutions.

COMEDIAN DECLARES JERRY SEINFELD 'UNCANCELLABLE' DESPITE 'WOKE' ANTI-ISRAEL FESTIVAL BOYCOTT

"Silencing artists because of government policies closes conversation. And don’t we need to keep that open?" Cohen said.

In 2025, over 1,000 Hollywood stars, directors and other film workers, including Emma Stone and Mark Ruffalo, signed a pledge to boycott institutions such as festivals, cinemas, broadcasters and production companies that "are implicated in genocide and apartheid against the Palestinian people."

Cohen denied films like "Our Loves" erased the Palestinian people and encouraged a more open mind.

HOLLYWOOD STARS LIKE MAYIM BIALIK, DEBRA MESSING AMONG 1,200 BLASTING ISRAELI FILM BOYCOTT AS 'ERASURE OF ART'

"I mean, you don’t have to agree with a government to hear the stories of its people," Cohen said.

In the meantime, she told The Hollywood Reporter she and several others are still grieving the losses of that day.

"You couldn’t really grieve until all the hostages were home," Cohen said. "So, really, we’re not even at the end of the first year of grieving. And there will be many more years."

'NOBODY WANTS THIS': CONSULTING RABBI CALLS OUT STAR'S 'IGNORANT' TAKE ON 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA

Cohen is perhaps best known for her portrayal as the Virgin Mary in Netflix's "Mary," which premiered in 2024. At the time, Cohen's casting caused an uproar among anti-Israel critics for casting an Israeli woman in the role, insisting that the real Mary was "Palestinian."

The film's director, D.J. Caruso, previously defended the casting in a statement, saying, "It was important to us that Mary, along with most of our primary cast, be selected from Israel to ensure authenticity."

In a comment to Fox News Digital, the Israeli-American Council (IAC) stood by Cohen's comments and called out efforts to target Israeli institutions and citizens.

"Artists have every right to express their views, including views we may strongly disagree with. But freedom of speech does not mean freedom to apply a double standard and engage in discrimination," the IAC said. 

"There is a clear difference between criticizing Israel's government policies and targeting Israeli artists because of their faith or national origin. Boycotting Israeli artists in the name of artistic freedom is disingenuous, wrong and a clear act of antisemitism."

item.title: DeSantis fraud crackdown drives nearly $1B spending plunge after providers billed impossible hours
item.description: Florida's Medicaid fraud crackdown uncovered providers billing for more than 24 hours a day, driving a nearly $1 billion drop in ABA therapy spending.
item.content:encoded:
Florida's sweeping Medicaid fraud crackdown has helped drive a nearly $1 billion reduction in projected annual spending on behavioral therapy services alone, according to state officials, after investigators uncovered suspicious billing practices.

Tallahassee’s internal crackdown — which included discoveries of providers billing Medicaid for more hours than there are in a day — comes amid heightened federal scrutiny of Medicaid fraud, including investigations and payment reviews involving Minnesota.

The DeSantis administration said its approach aims to stop suspicious Medicaid claims before taxpayer dollars are paid out rather than trying to recover improper payments afterward. The strategy mirrors a call from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to move away from traditional "pay-and-chase" models.

"This year, we announced the most significant Medicaid integrity initiative in the history of our state, and today, I was proud to announce some of the results from these efforts," Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news release.

VANCE TURNS UP HEAT ON STATES WITH FEDERAL CASH THREAT OVER MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN

More than 220 Medicaid providers have been terminated for fraud, waste or abuse, while more than 260 have faced payment restrictions or suspensions. The state has also referred more than 150 suspected fraud cases to the attorney general's office over the past year.

Annual Medicaid spending on Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA), a therapy commonly used for children with autism, had been projected to reach $3.86 billion but is now expected to total $2.88 billion in fiscal year 2026-27, according to the governor's office. Officials attributed the nearly $980 million reduction to a combination of fraud enforcement, managed care and utilization management efforts.

Florida's Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) told Fox News Digital that its expanded monitoring uncovered providers billing Medicaid for services through every weekend and holiday for months, including instances in which providers billed for more than 24 hours of services in a single day.

"Protecting Medicaid means protecting the people it was created to serve," AHCA Secretary Shevaun Harris said in a statement.

FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE'

"For children, pregnant women, the disabled, and our seniors, it means making sure they have access to high-quality care while ensuring taxpayer dollars are not lost to fraud or abuse. AHCA will continue taking decisive action to strengthen program integrity, hold bad actors accountable and safeguard these critical services for Floridians," she said.

Harris’ agency provided additional details on its crackdown to Fox News Digital, including how its new fraud-protection mechanisms work.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Through a pilot program with identity-verification firm SentiLink, Florida is screening for stolen or fake identities and hidden ownership structures among Medicaid providers. Separately, the state has imposed enrollment moratoriums on certain high-risk provider categories.

AHCA also told Fox News Digital that it has issued more than 1,000 adverse decisions involving Medicaid provider enrollment or re-enrollment since January 2026, part of its effort to prevent suspicious providers from entering or remaining in the program.

The agency has conducted 400 site visits to providers since January, including providers in high-risk categories such as applied behavior analysis, medical equipment and adult day care.

"Medicaid fraud is a national problem, and it is growing more sophisticated everywhere," AHCA told Fox News Digital.

"Florida is not waiting to be told what to do. We are building the model: prevent fraud at the front door, verify every provider, and follow the data. We welcome partnership with CMS and other states, because a fraudulent provider stopped in Florida is a scheme that does not move on to the next state."

item.title: Maryland man accused of girl's fatal shooting released from prison days before
item.description: Tyree Reynolds was released from prison just eight days before allegedly killing 12-year-old Khloe Ishway near a Baltimore youth football game.
item.content:encoded:
A Maryland man charged with killing a 12-year-old girl while allegedly firing at two men near a youth football game was released from prison just eight days before the deadly shooting.

Tyree Reynolds, 23, was released from state custody on Sept. 25, according to Fox 45 News, which cited the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (MDPSCS).

Reynolds faces 30 criminal counts, including murder and attempted murder, in connection with Saturday's shooting at a youth football homecoming game at Leon Day Park in Baltimore.

HOUSE DEMOCRAT BLASTED AFTER EARLY RELEASE LAW FREED INMATES LATER CHARGED WITH MURDER

During a Wednesday court appearance, Reynolds waived his bond hearing. He appeared via video from a wheelchair with a cast around his leg.

Authorities said surveillance footage captured Reynolds opening fire on two men in a parking lot adjacent to the football field during an argument over a parking spot. Investigators allege Reynolds reached into a backpack, pulled out a short-barreled rifle and began firing.

POLICE MAKE ARREST AFTER GUNFIRE DURING CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME LEAVES 1 DEAD

One of the men returned fire, striking Reynolds in the ankle. Reynolds then allegedly fired toward the football field, striking 12-year-old Khloe Ishway and three other victims.

Ishway died from her injuries.

"Khloe was just 12 years old. She should have a whole life ahead of her: school, a career, time spent with family and friends. Instead, she was killed because two adult men resorted to deadly violence to resolve an argument over a parking spot," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said.

"Our hearts remain with Khloe's mother, her family and friends, and our entire community, and we are committed to getting justice on their behalf," he continued.

CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

At the time of the shooting, Reynolds was on probation stemming from a previous shooting for which he had recently completed his prison sentence.

"The Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services is heartbroken by the tragic death of 12-year-old Khloe Ishway and the injuries to innocent bystanders," the agency said in a statement. "Tyree Reynolds was previously sentenced to 15 years of incarceration, with all but five years suspended by a judge. Reynolds served the entirety of that five-year term, day for day, and was released on September 25, 2026."

Reynolds was arrested three times in 2021. In February of that year, he was arrested on a handgun possession charge and was granted pretrial release.

Before he was sentenced in that case, Reynolds was arrested again in connection with a March 2021 assault and later in connection with a July 2021 shooting that was never prosecuted, according to Fox 45 News.

Reynolds later pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of first-degree assault and a firearms violation. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison, followed by three years of probation.

A judge suspended all but five years of the 15-year sentence, which Reynolds served in full before his release in September.

item.title: NFL calls prediction markets a form of sports gambling, urges courts to let states regulate
item.description: The National Football League filed an amicus brief arguing prediction markets like Kalshi should face state gambling regulation over game integrity.
item.content:encoded:
The National Football League has made its stance clear on prediction markets.

In an amicus brief on Thursday, the league said that the sites fall under the sports gambling umbrella and should similarly be regulated by states.

"Billions of dollars will be bet on NFL games through prediction markets each season, and any delay from the Court will result in increasing consumer harm and risk to game integrity," the NFL wrote in the brief, via ESPN.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The league sent a letter to prediction market operators just before the start of the season saying they objected to markets like coaching and officiating decisions, injuries, and other markets that could be swayed by insider info. The league has yet to partner with predict markets but does have deals with official online sportsbooks.

"The [Commodity Futures Trading] Commission's failure even to reference such objectionable contracts that the NFL identified months ago -- contracts that have been and continue to be listed as contracts by operators like Kalshi -- is deeply concerning and creates significant risks for the NFL's players, coaches, and officials and market participants," the league said.

The CFTC, however, said that it has been in touch with the league as prediction markets have risen, but the league has not entered an agreement with them to work together.

"Since day 1, the CFTC has engaged with the NFL regarding the agency’s rulemaking agenda and policy priorities. It’s unfortunate the NFL declined to sign an MOU with the CFTC which would’ve provided the league the ability to better discuss, cooperate, and exchange information with us to promote the integrity and resilience of prediction markets," Brooke Nethercott, public affairs director for the CFTC, told Fox News Digital.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

A CFTC source said that "just weeks ago, several senior NFL staff members notified senior CFTC staff that they were on the verge of commercial partnerships with several prediction market operators."

Kalshi also took a shot at the NFL for not being "willing to share data and collaborate to protect game integrity."

"Kalshi’s top priority is the integrity of its markets. That priority is reflected in the fact that other major sports league and integrity partner in the United States is partnering with Kalshi—including the MLB, NHL, USTA and others," Kalshi told Fox News Digital. "Contrary to the NFL’s statements, the CFTC is actively policing sports-related markets, which are now listed on nearly every US commodities exchange. The CFTC’s ongoing rulemaking addresses many of the NFL’s supposed concerns. And those rules sit atop the same comprehensive system of federal enforcement that protects trillions of dollars of transactions in US markets."

A source from the CFTC also said that the NFL's brief "makes clear that it is most interested in regulating the regulator, not game integrity."

"While this bullying tactic may work in the states, the CFTC will not be subject to regulatory capture, which is exactly why the federal framework established by Congress is the most effective way to regulate prediction markets," the source said.

"This is not about the NFL opposing prediction markets..." an NFL source said. "If the CFTC were to adopt the same robust regulatory approach as states, this would be less of an issue...

"For years, ever since sports betting on prediction markets started to gain traction, the NFL has been closely engaged in the relevant policy discussions. This is about protecting game integrity and consumers—just like legalized sports betting. There have already been billions of dollars in NFL wagers on prediction markets this season. Given this volume of trading and the uncertainty around it, it is critical for the Court to act as soon as possible. But it is unclear if the Commission has the resources or staff to adequately regulate sports betting."

"Polymarket shares the NFL’s commitment to preserving the integrity of the game, which is why we’ve built advanced market surveillance tools and are actively collaborating with the CFTC, SEC, and other professional leagues toward a harmonized federal framework that delivers a stronger, more consistent form of integrity compared to a patchwork of disconnected state laws built for a bygone era," a Polymarket spokesperson said.

The league's filing comes as New Jersey challenges a federal appeals court ruling that favored Kalshi's position that federal commodities law overrides state gambling regulations.

Prediction markets can be used by those 18 and older, while online sportsbooks are limited to those 21 and older.

Apple introduced Impersonation Risk Detection with iOS 27. The feature is designed to help with active social engineering scams, where someone pressures or guides you into doing something yourself. That last part is important. Traditional security can help block malware or stop an unauthorized login. However, those defenses can have a harder time helping when you are the legitimate account holder and a scammer has convinced you to send money or change sensitive account information.

When you perform certain sensitive actions inside a supported third-party app, that app can ask Apple for a risk assessment. Apple says examples may include making a payment or changing critical security information such as a password.

The app then receives one of three risk levels:

From there, the app decides how to respond. It might ask you to verify your identity, delay an action or display a warning before letting you continue. That could give you one more opportunity to stop when a scammer is rushing you through a payment or account change.

Impersonation Risk Detection looks at signals related to how you are using your device. Apple says those signals can include interaction patterns, timing, context and basic sensor data. Apple's privacy documentation gives some additional examples. Your iPhone may consider whether you are sharing your screen as well as the approximate number of recent phone calls or emails you have received. It can combine that assessment with certain Apple Account information, including recent App Store downloads and purchases.

The goal is to look for unusual behavior that could suggest someone is guiding or pressuring you. However, there is an important limitation. This feature works only with third-party apps that support Apple's Impersonation Risk Detection system. Turning it on does not give every app on your iPhone automatic scam detection.

Apple says it never analyzes the content of your Photos, Messages or Mail for this feature. The underlying device information used to create the assessment also stays protected from both Apple and the requesting app. There is still some information sharing you should understand before turning it on. Your iPhone creates an on-device assessment and sends that assessment, rather than the underlying device data, to Apple.

Apple can then combine it with certain Apple Account activity to generate the final risk signals. Apple also learns the category of activity you were attempting, such as signing in or making a payment. Apple says it does not learn which app requested the signals or the content of what you were doing inside the app. The requesting app receives the resulting risk level. It does not receive the underlying information Apple used to produce it.

Apple requires you to choose whether supported apps can request Impersonation Risk Detection signals. As a result, Share with App Developers starts out turned off. That means simply updating your iPhone to iOS 27 does not activate the protection. You need to go into Settings and enable it yourself.

One warning from Apple really stands out. If somebody on the phone tells you to disable Impersonation Risk Detection, Apple says you might be dealing with a scammer. I would treat a request like that as a major red flag. Hang up and contact the company using a number or app you already trust.

Here's how to check the setting on an iPhone running iOS 27:

Apple says changes to this setting may take up to 24 hours to take effect. After you turn it on, you can return to Settings > Privacy & Security > Impersonation Risk Detection to see which apps have recently requested a risk assessment. You can also review why each app requested access and turn off access for individual apps.

Samsung Galaxy phones also include tools designed to identify suspicious callers, although the exact features you see can vary by model, carrier and software version. On many Galaxy phones, Caller ID and spam protection is the main setting to check. Samsung uses technology from Hiya to identify suspected spam, scam and potential fraud calls, including numbers that aren't saved in your contacts.

Samsung also offers a separate real-time Scam detection feature on some compatible Galaxy phones running One UI 8.5 or higher. Samsung says that feature can analyze calls for scam patterns and alert you with a tone or vibration. However, that option does not appear on every Galaxy phone, even when the device is running current software. Samsung began rolling out One UI 9 in September 2026, starting with the Galaxy S26 series after its debut on Samsung's newest foldables. Feature availability can still depend on your model, carrier and region.

MAKE UNKNOWN CALLERS EXPLAIN WHY THEY'RE CALLING

On a Samsung Galaxy, the exact options can vary by model, carrier and software version. To check the protection available on your phone:

Samsung uses call-identification technology from Hiya to help identify suspected spam and scam callers, including numbers that aren't saved in your contacts. On compatible Galaxy phones, you may also see Call screening in the Phone app's settings. That feature can handle certain incoming calls before you answer. Samsung documents Call screening for compatible phones running One UI 8.5 or higher.

Google takes a different approach on Pixel phones. Its Scam Detection feature can analyze a phone conversation in real time and warn you when the call shows patterns commonly associated with fraud.

In the U.S., Google currently supports call Scam Detection on eligible Pixel 6 and later devices, with some model-specific exceptions. Pixel 9 and newer models use Gemini Nano on the device for scam detection during calls.

Google says the feature works on the device. However, the company also warns that it cannot detect every scam, so a call that receives no warning should never automatically be considered safe.

To check it:

Call Scam Detection requires you to opt in. If Google detects patterns associated with a scam during an eligible call, your Pixel can warn you while the conversation is still happening. That's useful because many scams become more convincing once a criminal gets you talking. The scammer can adjust the story based on what you say and keep applying pressure.

Pixel owners have another protection worth checking. Scam Detection for chat messages can analyze new message notifications from supported apps and warn you when something looks suspicious. Google says this feature is available in the U.S. and several other countries. In the U.S., Scam Detection can also work with Gboard in select messaging apps and warn you as you begin responding to a suspicious message. Google expanded that capability with its September 2026 Pixel update. Unlike call Scam Detection, message Scam Detection is turned on by default.

Google says the feature runs in a secure, isolated environment. Your message content stays private and is not sent to Google unless you choose to share a message after receiving an alert. Google's September 2026 Pixel update is rolling out to supported Pixel devices running Android 17, so I would also make sure your Pixel has the latest available system update installed.

SCAMMERS KNOW THE BEST TIME TO TEXT YOU

These features aren't interchangeable, which is actually helpful. Apple's Impersonation Risk Detection focuses on signs that you may be getting manipulated while performing sensitive actions inside supported apps. Pixel can watch for scam patterns during calls and suspicious messages. Samsung can analyze supported calls for scam patterns.

A scam may also move between several channels. Someone could text you first, get you on the phone and eventually convince you to open a legitimate banking app. Having protections at different points in that process gives your phone more opportunities to warn you before money or account information changes hands.

Treat a scam warning as a reason to stop and verify what is happening. Don't keep following the caller's instructions while trying to decide whether the warning is right.

Hang up if you're on a suspicious call. Then contact the bank, government agency or company directly using its official app, website or a phone number you already trust.

The same goes for payment alerts. Open your financial institution's official app yourself and check the account. Don't use a phone number or link supplied by the person who contacted you.

Also remember the reverse. No warning does not prove that a call, message or transaction is legitimate. Apple and Google both make clear that these systems can miss scams.

I like these features, but I would use them as another layer rather than my only protection. Scammers constantly change their scripts. They can spoof caller ID, impersonate companies you know and use personal information to make a fake story sound believable.

If someone unexpectedly asks for a password, verification code or payment, slow down. A demand to transfer money to a "safe account" should also send up an immediate warning sign.

Strong antivirus software can help protect against malicious links, phishing sites and malware that may appear alongside these scams. A password manager can also help by generating unique passwords and making it harder to reuse the same credentials across accounts. The phone can warn you. You still get the final say.

What I find most interesting about these scam protections is how close they're getting to the moment when someone might actually lose money. For years, we've relied heavily on spam filters and caller warnings to keep criminals away. Now our phones are starting to look for what happens after the conversation begins. Apple's approach in iOS 27 could be especially useful when a scammer has already convinced you to open a legitimate app and take action yourself. Pixel can warn about suspicious calls and messages, while some compatible Galaxy phones can detect scam patterns during calls.

Would you trust your phone enough to stop a payment after it warned you that you might be getting scammed, or would you still need to see more proof before changing course? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Fire alarm disrupts Northwestern 'October 7' play based on massacre survivor testimony
item.description: A fire alarm forced evacuation during Northwestern University's "October 7" play featuring Hamas attack survivor testimony at Cahn Auditorium.
item.content:encoded:
A fire alarm at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois interrupted a play recounting firsthand testimony from survivors of the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attacks on Tuesday night, forcing an evacuation of the auditorium during a performance intended to commemorate the victims ahead of the massacre's third anniversary.

The performance, titled "October 7," was hosted by Northwestern Hillel and featured verbatim testimony from survivors and eyewitnesses of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led terrorist attacks, which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in 251 hostages being taken into Gaza.

Northwestern Media Relations told Fox News Digital that the fire alarm was activated during the performance at Cahn Auditorium, prompting an evacuation and a police investigation.

"At approximately 8:12 p.m., a fire alarm at Cahn Auditorium was activated, which caused the evacuation of the building," a Northwestern Media Relations spokesperson said. "Upon a fire and police investigation, the building was determined safe, and guests invited back in. The event continued as planned and concluded at 9:45 p.m. The Northwestern University Police Department will continue their investigation."

FORMER HAMAS HOSTAGE COUNTERS HASAN PIKER’S UT AUSTIN EVENT WITH HER STORY OF SURVIVAL

A spokesperson for Campaign Against Antisemitism condemned the broader climate facing Jewish students on college campuses in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"Campuses have become radicalized, resulting in the ostracization of Jewish students on campus," the spokesperson said. "Universities in the U.S. and throughout the West have to take a stand against antisemitism on campus. Administrative leave is a start, but if the allegations are borne out, the consequences need to be severe. That’s what zero tolerance means."

The earliest widely circulated version of the video, which shows attendees evacuating the auditorium as a fire alarm sounded, was posted by Ann McElhinney, co-writer of the play "October 7," who said in her post that the alarm hit "even stronger because it’s already October 7 in Israel."

ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'

McElhinney's co-author and husband, Phelim McAleer, called for those responsible to face consequences in an interview with the Jewish News Syndicate on Wednesday.

"The people responsible must be found and prosecuted," McAleer said. "These people are demonic. Disrupting the truth, disrupting stories of tragedy and heroism. They should be ashamed of themselves. This just makes us all the more determined to take this play to every campus across America."

The Coalition Against Antisemitism at Northwestern (CAAN) shared a statement on its website, saying that the timing of the alarm was particularly troubling because the 2023 massacre began amid rocket attacks and air raid sirens warning Israeli civilians to seek shelter.

CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS

However, the group emphasized that investigators had not established whether the alarm was deliberately activated. It said the Cook County State's Attorney's Office Hate Crimes Unit was aware of the incident and called for authorities to examine whether antisemitic bias played a role.

The incident came less than a year after Northwestern reached a $75 million agreement with the Trump administration to resolve federal civil rights investigations involving allegations of antisemitism and discrimination on campus.

Under the November 2025 agreement, Northwestern committed to strengthening protections for Jewish students, implementing mandatory antisemitism training and maintaining policies governing demonstrations and disruptions of university activities.

The production, created by McAleer and McElhinney and directed by Jeff Gurner, previously ran off-Broadway and was performed at several universities, including Princeton, UCLA and Bowdoin College.

item.title: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in record-breaking feat
item.description: DonnaJean Wilde held an abdominal plank for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games, smashing her own Guinness world record by nearly 30 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
A 61-year-old Canadian grandmother broke the female abdominal plank world record after holding the position for five hours.

DonnaJean Wilde accomplished the feat at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah on Oct. 4, breaking her own record by nearly 30 minutes, Storyful reported.

Wilde’s plank began at 3:03 p.m. and ended at 8:03 p.m., with several judges rotating in and out of shifts during that period, a spokesperson for the World Senior Games told Storyful.

FITNESS INFLUENCER SAYS ONE SIMPLE HABIT CAN HELP ANYONE GET BACK IN SHAPE

Her previous record of 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds was set on March 21, 2004, at the Canadian high school where she once served as vice principal, according to the Guinness Book of World Records.

"To successfully achieve the record, the challenger’s forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times," Guinness states. 

"The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout," it also says.

FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG

"My elbows hurt pretty bad," Wilde said after completing the previous record. 

"I was so worried about losing my form, and I think that’s why my quads hurt because I was just really tense."

She shared with Guinness that the first two hours "went by quickly," but the next two hours were much more difficult.

"The last hour was the most challenging, just to stay focused and keep my form," she said.

During the last 30 minutes, she said she focused on "breathing, staying calm and not shaking."

Wilde first added planking to her daily routine years ago after breaking her wrist because she could perform the exercise while wearing a cast.

"I realized that I could read and do things when I was planking and fell in love with it," she said, according to the report.

Wilde shared some advice for others aiming to hold extended planks.

item.title: 'Generation COVID' explores the lasting toll of pandemic-era school closures
item.description: "Generation COVID" follows families across five states over four years, documenting how pandemic school closures still affect children's mental health.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE — An upcoming documentary examines the lasting toll of school closures six years after the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted classrooms nationwide.

"Generation COVID," directed by Jennifer Sey and Andrew James, follows children and families across California, New York, Oregon, Colorado and Connecticut as they grapple with the effects of pandemic-era school closures and mandates. The documentary was filmed over more than four years.

Sey told Fox News Digital that while much of the country appears ready to move on from the pandemic, many children are still struggling with its consequences.

NEWSOM'S ADMISSION THAT INFAMOUS COVID MOVE WAS 'INSANE' TRIGGERS VIRAL FURY: 'WE ALL TOLD YOU'

"It just feels to me like everyone wants to move on, and there’s really been no reckoning about what we did to young people in particular, and I wanted to create a record of that so that it never happens again," the XX-XY Athletics founder said.

Sey said she hopes the film offers a visual record of how school closures affected American children and encourages a different approach during any future pandemic.

LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

Sey lived in San Francisco for more than three decades and spoke out against the city’s prolonged shutdowns.

"I ended up having to leave San Francisco. I lost a career I'd spent 30 years building, but I continued to speak out in defense of children." 

After leaving her job in 2022, Sey began producing the documentary.

Sey, a former elite gymnast and national team member, said her commitment to protecting children is rooted in the abuse she experienced as a young athlete. She is also an Emmy-winning producer of "Athlete A," a documentary examining the Larry Nassar sexual abuse scandal and broader abuse within elite gymnastics.

"I ended up being the first whistleblower about abuse in elite gymnastics all the way back in 2008. And I really did it because I wish someone had stood up for me when I was a child. And the abuse that I suffered, I really did not come out of it for two decades after having left the sport. And, so, when I see that children are suffering, I can't help myself. I will fight for them.

"I feel like everyone's moved on, but the kids have not moved on."

Sey said her experiences have shaped her determination to continue speaking out for children.

HERE'S HOW THE CDC TRIED TO USE BAD SCIENCE TO CONVINCE PEOPLE TO WEAR MASKS DURING COVID

She also argued that children were "dehumanized" during the pandemic.

"They were models, they were cogs in a wheel, and we lost all sense of the humanity of a child, the need to be around other kids for their own development. We lost a sense of a child learning to speak that's 3 years old and being told if you don't wear a mask, you're going to kill your grandmother. Who tells a child that? Who tells a small child that? We inflicted fear."

The film examines the consequences of school closures and the censorship that Sey believes helped keep them in place. "Generation COVID" premieres Oct. 22 on SalemNOW.

item.title: Caitlin Clark says she blocks social media hate and enjoys hostile WNBA road crowds
item.description: Caitlin Clark condemned racist rhetoric and discrimination while revealing she can't remember the last time she read a direct message on social media.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark said she can't remember the last time she read a direct message on social media. She also enjoys getting booed by opposing fans.

Apparently, WNBA players can be the subject of an enormous amount of attention without volunteering to spend their entire day focusing on the worst aspects of it.

CAITLIN CLARK'S LOWEST-RATED PLAYOFF GAME STILL OUTDREW EVERY NON-FEVER FIRST-ROUND BROADCAST

During her season-ending news conference Thursday, Clark condemned "racist rhetoric" and "discrimination," praised passionate crowds and explained how she tries to manage the noise surrounding her.

It was a refreshingly sane approach to a subject that has produced far too much nonsense around the WNBA. Some players, and plenty of people covering them, should take notice.

The discussion began with a question about Kelsey Mitchell's comments on the attention that comes with being Clark's teammate. Clark said seeing teammates go through that upset her. She rejected people using her name to promote racism or discrimination.

"That's never been something I've stood for," Clark said. "For those of you that know me, that's not what I'm about. It's not how I was raised."

While Clark acknowledged that people shouldn't be sending nasty messages on social media, she said she tries to avoid reading them.

"I couldn't tell you the last time I read a direct message," Clark said. "I just try to block out the noise the best I can."

There is a useful lesson in that. Condemning someone else's behavior doesn't require giving that person unlimited access to your attention. Online trolls seek attention, which is why they send vile messages in the first place. Spending your time thinking about and reacting to those comments gives the trolls exactly what they want.

Clark recalled Golden State fans booing her every time she touched the ball.

"I like that. I thought that was great and fun," she said.

Imagine that. A professional athlete enjoying an opposing crowd trying to throw her off her game.

"You can boo. You can yell at people," Clark said. She even brought up watching the Yankees in the playoffs.

"Man, those Yankee fans are brutal," she said with a smile.

Anyone expecting a visiting star to receive a warm welcome in every building should probably spend a little more time watching sports. Those fans want to see their team win, and opponents are just standing in the way.

The atmosphere is part of what makes a road win satisfying. Enjoying it doesn't mean accepting everything fans say or do, as Clark made clear.

"I think there's certainly a line and that can't be crossed," she said, adding that "there's certain rhetoric that's just not okay."

Where that line falls became a major subject of debate during the playoffs, when Las Vegas Aces star A'ja Wilson confronted a Fever fan.

"You don’t step towards me. You never should step and point at me," Wilson said afterward.

Prime Video's broadcasters defended Wilson without knowing what the fan had said. Apparently, her reaction was all the evidence they needed.

But as OutKick reported, both the Fever and WNBA found no fan-conduct violation.

DAN DAKICH BLASTS A'JA WILSON OVER FAN INCIDENT IN PLAYOFF LOSS TO THE FEVER

Clark was discussing her own experiences Thursday. Still, her willingness to enjoy a hostile road crowd offers a useful perspective in a league where interactions with spectators have become such a consuming subject.

This wasn't the first time an opposing player accused a Fever fan of inappropriate conduct despite the team and league finding no such evidence.

Fever general manager Amber Cox said no fans had been removed for misconduct at home this season. Yet, left-wing podcaster Sarah Spain said Cox was being "defensive."

Well, wouldn't you be defensive if people kept trashing your fans and you had information that contradicted what they were saying?

Clark's answer showed how easily a person can condemn misconduct while also expressing appreciation for fans. Those positions fit together just fine.

"For the real fans that do show up and do support and do respect, I applaud you," she said. "And there are a lot of you. And that's not just here in Indianapolis. That's across the league."

When every conversation about fans revolves around the worst behavior, or the alleged worst behavior, the people who show up, support their teams and make the games worth watching can disappear from the discussion.

"There are a lot of really great fans and a lot of fans that I really, truly enjoy getting to play in front of," she said.

The rest of the WNBA would benefit from spending a little more time focusing on those people and a little less time reading DMs.
